projects.name: Serverless Image Processing Pipeline
projects.description: A production-grade serverless pipeline for uploading, processing, and serving images at scale. Uses S3, Lambda, Rekognition, RDS Aurora, and CloudFront — zero servers to manage.

why.title: Why the User?
why.text: The user uploads an image from a browser or mobile app. They receive a pre-signed S3 URL from the API which lets them upload directly to S3 — bypassing your servers entirely. This reduces latency and cost.

why.title: Why API Gateway?
why.text: API Gateway is a fully managed HTTP API endpoint. It handles authentication, rate limiting, and routing. Here it receives the upload request and triggers a Lambda to generate a pre-signed S3 URL.

why.title: Why S3?
why.text: S3 is AWS's object storage — infinitely scalable, 99.999999999% durable. Images are stored here both as originals and processed thumbnails. S3 Event Notifications trigger Lambda automatically when a new upload arrives.

why.title: Why Lambda for Processing?
why.text: Lambda is triggered automatically by S3 on every new upload. It resizes the image, converts formats, and calls Rekognition for AI analysis. Serverless means you pay only for the milliseconds it runs — no idle cost.

why.title: Why Rekognition?
why.text: AWS Rekognition is a fully managed AI/ML service for image analysis. It detects objects, scenes, faces, and inappropriate content. You pay per API call — no ML expertise or GPU servers required.

why.title: Why Aurora RDS?
why.text: Aurora Serverless is a relational database that auto-scales to zero when idle. We store image metadata — labels, dimensions, upload timestamps, user IDs — in structured SQL tables. Aurora Data API lets Lambda query it without managing connection pools.

why.title: Why CloudFront?
why.text: CloudFront is AWS's global CDN with 450+ edge locations worldwide. Images served via CloudFront are cached near the user — reducing latency from seconds to milliseconds. It also protects your S3 bucket from direct public access.

guide_steps.title: Architecture Overview
guide_steps.summary: Understand the serverless image pipeline before building it.

content.intro: This system handles image upload, AI processing, and global delivery — all without managing a single server. Let's understand the full picture first.
content.diagram:
User → API Gateway → S3 (upload)
S3 Event → Lambda → Rekognition (AI labels)
Lambda → Aurora RDS (store metadata)
User → CloudFront → S3 (serve image)

concepts.title: Event-Driven Architecture
concepts.text: Nothing polls or waits. S3 fires an event when an image arrives, Lambda wakes up instantly. This is reactive programming at the infrastructure level — pure pay-per-use.

concepts.title: Pre-signed URLs
concepts.text: Instead of routing the image through your API server (slow, expensive), you give the user a temporary URL to upload directly to S3. The URL expires in 5 minutes and is scoped to a single object.

concepts.title: Separation of Concerns
concepts.text: Upload, processing, storage, and delivery are completely decoupled services. You can swap CloudFront for another CDN or Rekognition for a custom model without touching the rest.

tradeoffs.pro: Zero infrastructure to manage or patch
tradeoffs.con: Cold starts on Lambda add 100-300ms latency on first invocation

tradeoffs.pro: Cost scales to zero when unused
tradeoffs.con: Vendor lock-in — tightly coupled to AWS services

tradeoffs.pro: Rekognition gives AI capabilities with no ML expertise
tradeoffs.con: Rekognition costs add up at high image volumes

guide_steps.title: S3 Bucket Setup
guide_steps.summary: Create the S3 bucket with correct permissions and event notifications.

content.intro: S3 is the heart of this system. All images land here. We need two prefixes: uploads/ (originals) and processed/ (thumbnails). S3 events will wake up Lambda automatically.
content.code:
# Create the bucket
aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket my-images-bucket \
  --region $AWS_REGION \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=$AWS_REGION

# Block all public access (CloudFront will serve images)
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket my-images-bucket \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
    BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,\
    BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

# Enable versioning for safety
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket my-images-bucket \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# Add S3 event notification to trigger Lambda on upload
aws s3api put-bucket-notification-configuration \
  --bucket my-images-bucket \
  --notification-configuration file://s3-notification.json

concepts.title: Block Public Access
concepts.text: Never make S3 buckets public directly. CloudFront uses an Origin Access Control (OAC) to fetch from S3 privately. This prevents data leaks and hotlinking.

concepts.title: S3 Event Notifications
concepts.text: s3:ObjectCreated:* fires for every new upload. You filter by prefix (uploads/) so Lambda only triggers on originals, not on processed thumbnails it writes back.

concepts.title: Object Key Convention
concepts.text: Use a predictable key structure: uploads/{userId}/{timestamp}-{filename}. This makes IAM path-based policies simple and enables per-user lifecycle rules.

tradeoffs.pro: Unlimited storage — no capacity planning needed
tradeoffs.con: No native directory structure — key prefixes simulate folders

tradeoffs.pro: S3 events are free and near-instant
tradeoffs.con: Event delivery is eventually consistent — rare duplicate events possible

guide_steps.title: Lambda Processor
guide_steps.summary: Write the Lambda that resizes images and calls Rekognition.

content.intro: The processor Lambda is the brain. It reads the uploaded image from S3, resizes it to a thumbnail, calls Rekognition for AI labels, then writes results to Aurora and the processed image back to S3.
content.code:
# Create Lambda execution role
aws iam create-role \
  --role-name lambda-image-processor-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://lambda-trust-policy.json

aws iam attach-role-policy \
  --role-name lambda-image-processor-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole

aws iam put-role-policy \
  --role-name lambda-image-processor-role \
  --policy-name ImageProcessorPolicy \
  --policy-document file://processor-policy.json

# Deploy the Lambda
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name image-processor \
  --runtime nodejs20.x \
  --role arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:role/lambda-image-processor-role \
  --handler index.handler \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip \
  --timeout 30 \
  --memory-size 512 \
  --environment Variables='{DB_CLUSTER_ARN=$DB_ARN,DB_SECRET_ARN=$SECRET_ARN}'
content.verify: aws lambda invoke --function-name image-processor --payload file://test-event.json response.json && cat response.json

concepts.title: Memory = CPU
concepts.text: Lambda allocates CPU proportionally to memory. Image processing is CPU-intensive — 512MB gives decent performance. 1769MB = 1 full vCPU.

concepts.title: Timeout Planning
concepts.text: Set timeout to 3x your expected execution time. A 1MB image typically processes in 3-5 seconds. We set 30s as a safety margin.

concepts.title: Layer for Sharp (image lib)
concepts.text: Use a Lambda Layer for native image processing libraries like Sharp. Layers are shared across functions and keep your deployment package small.

tradeoffs.pro: Scales from 0 to 1000 concurrent executions automatically
tradeoffs.con: 15-minute max execution limit — not suitable for video processing

tradeoffs.pro: No server to patch or maintain
tradeoffs.con: Cold starts add latency — use Provisioned Concurrency for latency-sensitive flows

guide_steps.title: Rekognition Integration
guide_steps.summary: Add AI-powered image analysis with zero ML infrastructure.

content.intro: AWS Rekognition analyzes images and returns labels (objects, scenes), moderation flags (adult/violent content), and confidence scores. One API call, no model training required.
content.code:
# Test Rekognition directly against an S3 object
aws rekognition detect-labels \
  --image '{"S3Object":{"Bucket":"my-images-bucket","Name":"uploads/test.jpg"}}' \
  --max-labels 10 \
  --min-confidence 75 \
  --region $AWS_REGION

# Test content moderation
aws rekognition detect-moderation-labels \
  --image '{"S3Object":{"Bucket":"my-images-bucket","Name":"uploads/test.jpg"}}' \
  --min-confidence 60 \
  --region $AWS_REGION
content.verify: aws rekognition describe-project-versions --project-arn $PROJECT_ARN --region $AWS_REGION 2>/dev/null || echo 'Using standard Rekognition APIs'

concepts.title: Confidence Scores
concepts.text: Every label comes with a confidence percentage (0-100). Set min-confidence to 75+ for production — lower values produce noisy results.

concepts.title: Content Moderation
concepts.text: DetectModerationLabels returns a hierarchy: Explicit Nudity > Nudity > Graphic Male Nudity etc. Store the top-level category in your DB for fast filtering.

concepts.title: Billing Model
concepts.text: Rekognition charges per image analyzed (~$0.001 per image after free tier). For 1M images/month: ~$1,000. Compare to training and hosting your own model.

tradeoffs.pro: No ML expertise needed — call an API, get results
tradeoffs.con: Black box — you cannot inspect or retrain the model

tradeoffs.pro: Handles massive scale with no infrastructure
tradeoffs.con: Costs increase linearly — at 10M+ images/month, custom models may be cheaper

guide_steps.title: Aurora Serverless DB
guide_steps.summary: Store image metadata in a serverless relational database.

content.intro: Aurora Serverless v2 auto-scales from minimum capacity to handle traffic spikes, and scales back to near-zero when idle. The Data API lets Lambda query it without managing connection pools.
content.code:
# Create Aurora Serverless v2 cluster
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --db-cluster-identifier images-db \
  --engine aurora-mysql \
  --engine-version 8.0.mysql_aurora.3.04.0 \
  --serverless-v2-scaling-configuration MinCapacity=0.5,MaxCapacity=4 \
  --master-username admin \
  --manage-master-user-password \
  --enable-http-endpoint \
  --region $AWS_REGION

# Create the images metadata table (run via Data API)
aws rds-data execute-statement \
  --resource-arn $DB_CLUSTER_ARN \
  --secret-arn $SECRET_ARN \
  --database images \
  --sql "CREATE TABLE images (
    id VARCHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    s3_key VARCHAR(1024) NOT NULL,
    thumbnail_key VARCHAR(1024),
    labels JSON,
    moderation_flags JSON,
    width INT, height INT,
    file_size_bytes INT,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    INDEX idx_user_id (user_id)
  );"

concepts.title: Serverless v2 ACUs
concepts.text: Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) define compute + memory. 0.5 ACU = minimum (saves cost at low traffic). Each ACU ~ 2GB RAM. For image metadata queries, 0.5-1 ACU is plenty.

concepts.title: HTTP Endpoint (Data API)
concepts.text: Lambda can query Aurora over HTTPS using the Data API — no VPC, no connection pooling. This is perfect for serverless since Lambda doesn't maintain persistent DB connections.

concepts.title: JSON Column for Labels
concepts.text: Storing Rekognition labels as JSON lets you add new label types without schema migrations. You can still query them with MySQL JSON functions: WHERE JSON_CONTAINS(labels, '"Dog"').

tradeoffs.pro: Scales to zero — pay almost nothing when idle
tradeoffs.con: Cold start when scaling from zero adds ~5 seconds latency

tradeoffs.pro: Fully managed — automated backups, multi-AZ failover
tradeoffs.con: Data API has a 1MB response limit — not suitable for large result sets

guide_steps.title: CloudFront CDN
guide_steps.summary: Serve images globally with low latency via a CDN.

content.intro: CloudFront caches your S3 images at 450+ edge locations worldwide. A user in Tokyo gets an image from a Tokyo edge node, not your S3 bucket in us-east-1. Setup takes 15 minutes and costs almost nothing.
content.code:
# Create Origin Access Control (replaces legacy OAI)
aws cloudfront create-origin-access-control \
  --origin-access-control-config \
    Name=images-oac,OriginAccessControlOriginType=s3,\
    SigningBehavior=always,SigningProtocol=sigv4

# Create the distribution
aws cloudfront create-distribution \
  --distribution-config file://cf-distribution.json

# Update S3 bucket policy to allow only CloudFront
aws s3api put-bucket-policy \
  --bucket my-images-bucket \
  --policy file://s3-bucket-policy.json

# Invalidate cache after processing (call from Lambda)
aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id $CF_DIST_ID \
  --paths '/processed/*'

concepts.title: Origin Access Control (OAC)
concepts.text: OAC is the modern way to let CloudFront access S3 privately. It uses SigV4 signing — more secure than the legacy Origin Access Identity (OAI). S3 bucket stays fully private.

concepts.title: Cache Behaviors
concepts.text: Configure TTL per path prefix. Cache /processed/* for 30 days (immutable thumbnails). Cache /uploads/* for 1 hour. Use Cache-Control headers from Lambda for fine-grained control.

concepts.title: Cache Invalidation
concepts.text: After Lambda processes an image and writes the thumbnail, invalidate the CloudFront path so the next request fetches the new file. First 1,000 invalidations/month are free.

tradeoffs.pro: Sub-50ms image delivery worldwide
tradeoffs.con: Cache invalidation can take up to 60 seconds to propagate globally

tradeoffs.pro: Reduces S3 GET request costs dramatically
tradeoffs.con: CloudFront has its own data transfer costs — analyze at scale

projects.name: Job Processing System
projects.description: A production-grade async job processing pipeline using EC2, SQS, DynamoDB, Lambda and ECR. Learn how to decouple services and handle failures with Dead Letter Queues.

why.title: Why a Client?
why.text: The client is anyone sending a request to the API — a website, mobile app, or a curl command in the terminal. It sends an HTTP request and receives a response containing a Job ID.

why.title: Why EC2 for the API?
why.text: EC2 gives us a virtual server with full control over the OS. The API runs as a Docker Container on EC2, accepting HTTP requests on port 8080. It saves the Job to DynamoDB and publishes a message to SQS.

why.title: Why DynamoDB?
why.text: DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database — AWS handles all maintenance, scaling, and backups. It offers millisecond latency and a generous free tier (25 read/write capacity units). We store all Jobs here with their current status.

why.title: Why SQS?
why.text: SQS is a message queue — think of it as a post office box. The API drops messages in, and the Worker picks them up. This is called Decoupling: the API doesn't wait for the Worker to finish. If the Worker crashes, messages safely wait in the queue.

why.title: Why a separate Worker?
why.text: The Worker runs as a separate Docker Container (on the same or different EC2). It polls SQS for messages and processes them. Keeping it separate enables independent scaling — add more Workers without touching the API.

why.title: Why a Dead Letter Queue?
why.text: The DLQ holds messages that failed processing 3 times (Redrive Policy). Instead of retrying infinitely, failed messages are moved here for investigation. This keeps the main queue clean and prevents poison-pill messages from blocking other jobs.

why.title: Why Lambda?
why.text: Lambda is serverless compute — no server to manage! It runs automatically when a message arrives in the DLQ. It updates DynamoDB to mark the job as FAILED. You pay only for execution time (milliseconds), making it perfect for rare error-handling tasks.

guide_steps.title: Architecture Overview
guide_steps.summary: Understand the full data flow before building anything.

content.intro: Before writing a single CLI command, understand what we're building and why each service exists.
content.diagram:
Client → API (EC2) → DynamoDB (store job) → SQS (send message)
                   
Worker (EC2) ← SQS (receive message) → DynamoDB (update job status)
           
DLQ (SQS) → Lambda → DynamoDB (mark as failed)

concepts.title: Loosely Coupled Architecture
concepts.text: Services communicate through AWS APIs, not direct connections. The API doesn't call the Worker directly — it drops a message in SQS and moves on. This is called async/event-driven architecture.

concepts.title: Managed Services
concepts.text: DynamoDB, SQS, and Lambda are fully managed — AWS handles servers, updates, backups, and scaling. You configure and use them. Compare: DynamoDB vs. MySQL on EC2 (you'd manage the DB server yourself).

concepts.title: The Cloud Mental Model
concepts.text: Old way: Buy a car, maintain it, insure it. Cloud way: Use Uber — pay per ride, zero maintenance. AWS lets you rent compute, storage, and queuing instead of owning the hardware.

tradeoffs.pro: API responds instantly — doesn't wait for job processing
tradeoffs.con: More complex architecture to debug

tradeoffs.pro: Worker failures don't affect the API or user experience
tradeoffs.con: Eventual consistency — job status updates are not immediate

tradeoffs.pro: Each component scales independently
tradeoffs.con: More AWS services to learn and manage

guide_steps.title: DynamoDB Table
guide_steps.summary: Create the NoSQL database that stores all job records.

content.intro: DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database. Think of it as a giant key-value store where each row can have different attributes.
content.whyThis: We chose DynamoDB over running MySQL on EC2 because we don't want to manage a database server. AWS handles replication, backups, and scaling automatically.
content.code:
aws dynamodb create-table \
    --table-name Jobs \
    --attribute-definitions \
        AttributeName=jobId,AttributeType=S \
        AttributeName=idempotencyKey,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema \
        AttributeName=jobId,KeyType=HASH \
    --global-secondary-indexes \
        'IndexName=idempotencyKey-index,\
        KeySchema=[{AttributeName=idempotencyKey,KeyType=HASH}],\
        Projection={ProjectionType=ALL},\
        ProvisionedThroughput={ReadCapacityUnits=5,WriteCapacityUnits=5}' \
    --billing-mode PROVISIONED \
    --provisioned-throughput ReadCapacityUnits=5,WriteCapacityUnits=5 \
    --region $AWS_REGION

concepts.title: Primary Key (jobId)
concepts.text: Every item in DynamoDB needs a unique primary key. jobId is our HASH key — like a row ID in SQL.

concepts.title: Global Secondary Index
concepts.text: Allows querying by idempotencyKey. Without this index, you'd have to scan the entire table — expensive and slow.

concepts.title: Provisioned vs On-Demand
concepts.text: PROVISIONED mode: you specify capacity upfront (free tier: 25 RCU/WCU). ON_DEMAND: pay per request, auto-scales. We use PROVISIONED to stay in free tier.

tradeoffs.pro: No server management — AWS handles everything
tradeoffs.con: NoSQL means no JOINs — data model must be designed carefully

tradeoffs.pro: Millisecond latency at any scale
tradeoffs.con: Querying non-primary-key fields requires a GSI (extra cost/complexity)

tradeoffs.pro: Serverless billing — pay per request with On-Demand
tradeoffs.con: Provisioned capacity can be wasted if traffic is unpredictable

guide_steps.title: SQS Queues
guide_steps.summary: Set up the message queue and dead letter queue for async job processing.

content.intro: SQS is a message queue — like a post office. The API puts messages in, the Worker takes them out. Messages wait safely even if the Worker is down.
content.whyThis: We chose SQS over running RabbitMQ on EC2 because SQS is serverless — no broker to manage, patch, or scale. It stores messages durably until processed.
content.code:
# Create main queue
aws sqs create-queue \
    --queue-name jobs-queue \
    --attributes VisibilityTimeout=300,MessageRetentionPeriod=1209600 \
    --region $AWS_REGION

# Create Dead Letter Queue
aws sqs create-queue \
    --queue-name jobs-dlq \
    --attributes MessageRetentionPeriod=1209600 \
    --region $AWS_REGION

# Connect DLQ to main queue (after 3 failed attempts)
aws sqs set-queue-attributes \
    --queue-url "$QUEUE_URL" \
    --attributes '{"RedrivePolicy":"{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"$DLQ_ARN\",\"maxReceiveCount\":3}"}' \
    --region $AWS_REGION

concepts.title: Visibility Timeout (300s)
concepts.text: When a Worker reads a message, it becomes invisible to other Workers for 5 minutes. If not deleted in time (job failed), it reappears for retry.

concepts.title: Message Retention (14 days)
concepts.text: Messages are kept for 14 days if not processed. Useful if your Worker is down for a while — no messages are lost.

concepts.title: Redrive Policy (maxReceiveCount=3)
concepts.text: After 3 failed processing attempts, the message is automatically moved to the DLQ. This prevents infinite retry loops from blocking your queue.

tradeoffs.pro: Messages persist even if Worker crashes
tradeoffs.con: At-least-once delivery — Workers must be idempotent (same message processed twice = same result)

tradeoffs.pro: Decouples API from Worker — independent scaling
tradeoffs.con: Not real-time — there's a small delay between enqueue and process

tradeoffs.pro: DLQ catches poison-pill messages automatically
tradeoffs.con: Max message size is 256KB — large payloads need S3 + pointer pattern

guide_steps.title: ECR Repositories
guide_steps.summary: Create private Docker image registries for the API and Worker.

content.intro: ECR (Elastic Container Registry) is AWS's private Docker registry. Think of it as Docker Hub, but private and integrated with AWS IAM.
content.whyThis: We use ECR instead of Docker Hub because ECR integrates natively with IAM — no credentials needed when pulling images from EC2. It's also private by default.
content.code:
# Get your AWS account ID
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)

# Create API repository
aws ecr create-repository \
    --repository-name svc-api \
    --region $AWS_REGION

# Create Worker repository
aws ecr create-repository \
    --repository-name svc-worker \
    --region $AWS_REGION

# Build and push images
aws ecr get-login-password --region $AWS_REGION | \
    docker login --username AWS --password-stdin \
    $ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_REGION.amazonaws.com

docker build -t svc-api:latest ./services/svc-api
docker tag svc-api:latest $ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_REGION.amazonaws.com/svc-api:latest
docker push $ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_REGION.amazonaws.com/svc-api:latest

concepts.title: Docker Images as Shipping Containers
concepts.text: A Docker image packages your app + all dependencies. It runs identically on your laptop, CI/CD, and EC2. 'Works on my machine' problem: solved.

concepts.title: IAM-based Pull Auth
concepts.text: EC2 with the right IAM role can pull ECR images without any credentials. AWS handles token rotation automatically via the instance metadata service.

concepts.title: Image Tags
concepts.text: We use :latest for simplicity. In production, use commit SHA tags (e.g., :abc1234) for reproducible deploys and easy rollbacks.

tradeoffs.pro: IAM-integrated — no credential management for EC2 pulls
tradeoffs.con: Cross-region pulls are slow and cost egress fees

tradeoffs.pro: Private by default — no accidental public exposure
tradeoffs.con: Costs $0.10/GB storage (small images are essentially free)

tradeoffs.pro: Lifecycle policies can auto-delete old images
tradeoffs.con: Requires Docker installed locally to build and push

guide_steps.title: IAM Roles & Policies
guide_steps.summary: Define what each service is allowed to do — the Principle of Least Privilege.

content.intro: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is AWS's permission system. It controls who can do what. This is the most security-critical step.
content.whyThis: Without IAM, any service could access any resource. A compromised EC2 instance could delete your database. IAM limits blast radius by granting minimum necessary permissions.
content.code:
# Create EC2 trust policy (who can assume this role)
cat > /tmp/ec2-trust-policy.json <<EOF
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
  }]
}
EOF

# Create role
aws iam create-role \
    --role-name jobsys-ec2-role \
    --assume-role-policy-document file:///tmp/ec2-trust-policy.json

# Attach permissions policy (DynamoDB + SQS + SSM + ECR)
aws iam put-role-policy \
    --role-name jobsys-ec2-role \
    --policy-name jobsys-ec2-policy \
    --policy-document file:///tmp/ec2-policy.json

# Create instance profile (so EC2 can use the role)
aws iam create-instance-profile \
    --instance-profile-name jobsys-ec2-role

aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile \
    --instance-profile-name jobsys-ec2-role \
    --role-name jobsys-ec2-role

concepts.title: Trust Policy vs Permission Policy
concepts.text: Trust policy: WHO can use this role (e.g., EC2 service). Permission policy: WHAT that role can do (e.g., SQS:SendMessage). Both are required.

concepts.title: Instance Profile → IMDS
concepts.text: EC2 gets temporary credentials via the Instance Metadata Service at 169.254.169.254. Your app calls AWS SDKs — they automatically fetch credentials from IMDS. Zero hardcoded keys.

concepts.title: Principle of Least Privilege
concepts.text: Grant only the minimum permissions needed. The API can SendMessage to SQS but cannot DeleteQueue. If the API is compromised, the attacker can't destroy infrastructure.

tradeoffs.pro: No hardcoded credentials — temporary tokens auto-rotate every ~6 hours
tradeoffs.con: IAM policies can be complex — easy to make overly permissive mistakes

tradeoffs.pro: Fine-grained control per service (API vs Worker vs Lambda)
tradeoffs.con: Resource ARNs must be exact — wildcard (*) opens security holes

tradeoffs.pro: CloudTrail audits every API call made by each role
tradeoffs.con: Debugging IAM denials can be frustrating — use IAM Policy Simulator

guide_steps.title: EC2 Instance
guide_steps.summary: Launch a virtual server to run the API and Worker containers.

content.intro: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is a virtual server in the cloud. You choose the OS, instance type, and configuration. Your Docker containers run here.
content.whyThis: We use EC2 because our API and Worker are long-running processes. Lambda has a 15-minute timeout and cold starts. EC2 gives us full control and predictable performance.
content.code:
# Get default VPC
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs \
    --filters "Name=isDefault,Values=true" \
    --query 'Vpcs[0].VpcId' --output text)

# Create security group (firewall)
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group \
    --group-name jobsys-ec2-sg \
    --description "Security group for jobsys" \
    --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" \
    --query 'GroupId' --output text)

# Allow SSH from your IP only
MY_IP=$(curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
    --group-id "$SG_ID" --protocol tcp \
    --port 22 --cidr "$MY_IP/32"

# Allow API traffic from anywhere
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
    --group-id "$SG_ID" --protocol tcp \
    --port 8080 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# Launch instance (t3.micro = free tier)
INSTANCE_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances \
    --image-id "$AMI_ID" \
    --instance-type t3.micro \
    --security-group-ids "$SG_ID" \
    --iam-instance-profile Name=jobsys-ec2-role \
    --user-data file:///tmp/user-data.sh \
    --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)

concepts.title: Security Groups as Firewalls
concepts.text: Security groups are stateful firewalls. We only open port 22 (SSH) from our IP and port 8080 for the API. All other traffic is denied by default.

concepts.title: User Data Script
concepts.text: A bash script that runs once on first boot. We use it to install Docker, pull images from ECR, and start our containers automatically.

concepts.title: t3.micro (Free Tier)
concepts.text: 750 hours/month free for 12 months. t3.micro = 2 vCPUs + 1GB RAM. Enough for learning. In production, right-size based on load testing.

tradeoffs.pro: Full OS control — install anything, any runtime
tradeoffs.con: You manage OS patching, Docker updates, and app restarts

tradeoffs.pro: Persistent — always running, no cold starts
tradeoffs.con: Costs money even when idle (vs Lambda which is pay-per-invocation)

tradeoffs.pro: Familiar deployment model for most developers
tradeoffs.con: Horizontal scaling requires Load Balancer + Auto Scaling Group setup

guide_steps.title: Lambda + DLQ Handler
guide_steps.summary: Create a serverless function triggered automatically by the Dead Letter Queue.

content.intro: Lambda is serverless compute — write a function, AWS runs it. No server to provision, patch, or manage. Perfect for event-driven tasks like handling failed jobs.
content.whyThis: We use Lambda for DLQ processing because it only runs when there's a failed message. Running a dedicated EC2 instance 24/7 for rare failure events would be wasteful and expensive.
content.code:
# Create Lambda IAM role
aws iam create-role \
    --role-name dlq-handler-role \
    --assume-role-policy-document file:///tmp/lambda-trust-policy.json

# Attach DynamoDB + CloudWatch permissions
aws iam put-role-policy \
    --role-name dlq-handler-role \
    --policy-name dlq-handler-policy \
    --policy-document file:///tmp/lambda-policy.json

# Create Lambda function from zip
aws lambda create-function \
    --function-name dlq-handler \
    --runtime python3.11 \
    --role "$LAMBDA_ROLE_ARN" \
    --handler lambda_function.lambda_handler \
    --zip-file fileb://dlq-handler.zip \
    --timeout 30 \
    --memory-size 256 \
    --environment "Variables={DDB_TABLE=Jobs}"

# Connect DLQ → Lambda (event source mapping)
aws lambda create-event-source-mapping \
    --function-name dlq-handler \
    --event-source-arn "$DLQ_ARN" \
    --batch-size 1
content.verify:
aws lambda get-function --function-name dlq-handler
aws lambda list-event-source-mappings --function-name dlq-handler

concepts.title: Event Source Mapping
concepts.text: This is the 'wire' between DLQ and Lambda. When a message arrives in the DLQ, Lambda is triggered automatically. No polling code needed — AWS manages this.

concepts.title: Lambda Cold Starts
concepts.text: First invocation after inactivity takes longer (cold start). For our DLQ handler, this is fine — a few hundred ms delay on rare error events is acceptable.

concepts.title: Concurrency & Scaling
concepts.text: Lambda auto-scales to handle multiple messages simultaneously. Each invocation is isolated. With batch-size=1, each message gets its own Lambda execution.

tradeoffs.pro: Zero infrastructure management — just upload code
tradeoffs.con: 15-minute max timeout — not suitable for long-running jobs

tradeoffs.pro: Pay only when invoked — essentially free for rare DLQ events
tradeoffs.con: Cold starts can add latency (mitigate with Provisioned Concurrency)

tradeoffs.pro: Auto-scales to zero — no idle cost
tradeoffs.con: Local filesystem is ephemeral — use /tmp (512MB) or S3 for files

guide_steps.title: Testing the System
guide_steps.summary: Verify each component works and trace a job through the full pipeline.

content.intro: Test each layer: create a job, watch it flow through SQS to the Worker, verify DynamoDB updates, and test the DLQ failure path.
content.whyThis: End-to-end testing confirms all IAM permissions are correct, services can communicate, and your Redrive Policy works as expected.
content.code:
# Replace with your EC2 public IP
API_URL="http://$PUBLIC_IP:8080"

# Test 1: Create a job
curl -X POST "$API_URL/api/v1/jobs" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: test-$(date +%s)" \
  -d '{
    "type": "process_document",
    "priority": "normal",
    "params": { "source": "s3://bucket/test.pdf" }
  }'

# Test 2: Check job status (use jobId from above)
curl "$API_URL/api/v1/jobs/$JOB_ID"
# Expected: PENDING → PROCESSING → SUCCEEDED

# Test 3: Verify in DynamoDB directly
aws dynamodb get-item \
    --table-name Jobs \
    --key "{\"jobId\":{\"S\":\"$JOB_ID\"}}"

# Test 4: Check SQS queue depth
aws sqs get-queue-attributes \
    --queue-url "$QUEUE_URL" \
    --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessages
content.verify:
# Watch Worker logs in real-time
aws logs tail /aws/jobsys/svc-worker --follow --region $AWS_REGION

concepts.title: Idempotency Key
concepts.text: The Idempotency-Key header prevents duplicate jobs. If you retry the same request (network timeout), the API returns the existing job instead of creating a new one. DynamoDB's conditional writes enforce this.

concepts.title: Status Transitions
concepts.text: PENDING → PROCESSING → SUCCEEDED (or FAILED). Each transition is a DynamoDB UpdateItem call. The API sets PENDING, Worker sets PROCESSING then SUCCEEDED, Lambda sets FAILED.

concepts.title: CloudWatch Logs
concepts.text: All logs from EC2 containers and Lambda are in CloudWatch. Use 'aws logs tail' for real-time debugging without SSH-ing into instances.

tradeoffs.pro: Idempotency prevents duplicate processing on retry
tradeoffs.con: Idempotency keys must be stored — adds DB storage and lookup cost

tradeoffs.pro: Async polling is simple to implement for clients
tradeoffs.con: Clients must poll for status — consider WebSockets or SNS notifications for real-time UX

tradeoffs.pro: CloudWatch gives centralized logs for all services
tradeoffs.con: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries cost money — use log levels to filter noise

questions.question: Why store Rekognition labels in a JSON column in Aurora rather than normalizing them into separate SQL rows?
options: JSON columns are faster than relational rows for all queries
Labels vary unpredictably per image — JSON avoids schema migrations when Rekognition adds new label types
Aurora doesn't support multi-row inserts from Lambda
Rekognition returns labels in JSON and Aurora cannot parse other formats
questions.explanation: Image labels are variable and schema-less — a photo of a dog has different labels than a cityscape. Storing as JSON avoids creating a separate labels table with complex joins, while MySQL's JSON functions still allow querying label content.

questions.question: What is the minimum confidence threshold recommended for Rekognition label detection in production?
options: 10% — capture all possible labels
50% — balanced precision and recall
75%+ — reduces noise from low-confidence false detections
99% — only accept near-certain labels
questions.explanation: Setting min-confidence to 75+ filters out noisy, low-confidence detections. Below 75%, Rekognition often returns vague or incorrect labels that pollute your metadata database.

questions.question: What is a Lambda cold start and when does it occur?
options: When Lambda runs out of memory and restarts
The initial latency when Lambda spins up a new execution environment after being idle
Every invocation starts cold — Lambda never reuses environments
Cold starts only happen with VPC-attached Lambdas
questions.explanation: A cold start happens when Lambda needs to initialize a new execution environment (download code, start runtime). Subsequent invocations reuse the warm environment. Use Provisioned Concurrency to eliminate cold starts for latency-sensitive endpoints.

questions.question: What is Origin Access Control (OAC) in CloudFront and why is it preferred over the legacy OAI?
options: OAC is a caching policy; OAI is a routing policy
OAC uses SigV4 signing for stronger security and supports newer S3 features; OAI is legacy and less secure
OAC is faster because it bypasses S3 authentication
OAC and OAI are identical — just renamed
questions.explanation: OAC replaced OAI as the recommended way for CloudFront to access private S3 buckets. It uses AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4), supports SSE-KMS encrypted buckets, and is the current AWS best practice.

questions.question: Why does Aurora Serverless use the Data API instead of a standard TCP database connection from Lambda?
options: Lambda cannot make TCP connections
The Data API is faster than TCP for SQL queries
Lambda functions are stateless and short-lived — managing persistent DB connection pools is wasteful and complex
Standard DB connections require a VPC which Lambda doesn't support
questions.explanation: Traditional DB connections are persistent and stateful. Lambda spins up/down rapidly, making connection pool management a nightmare. The Aurora Data API uses HTTPS — no persistent connection, no VPC required, Lambda-friendly.

questions.question: Which IAM principle should govern the Lambda Processor's permissions?
options: Grant AdministratorAccess for simplicity in development
Grant only the specific S3 paths, Rekognition actions, and RDS cluster needed — nothing more
Grant full S3 and RDS access since Lambda is internal
No IAM role needed since Lambda is a managed service
questions.explanation: Least privilege means granting only what's needed. The Lambda needs s3:GetObject/PutObject on the specific bucket, rekognition:DetectLabels on *, and rds-data:ExecuteStatement on the specific cluster ARN.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Lambda memory and CPU performance?
options: CPU is always fixed at 1 vCPU regardless of memory
Higher memory only affects RAM, not processing speed
Lambda allocates CPU proportionally to memory — more memory = more CPU
CPU scales based on the number of concurrent invocations
questions.explanation: AWS allocates CPU proportionally to memory setting. At 1769MB you get 1 full vCPU. For CPU-intensive tasks like image resizing, increasing memory directly speeds up processing.

questions.question: Why should you block all public access on the S3 bucket and use CloudFront instead?
options: S3 public buckets are slower than CloudFront
CloudFront requires private S3 buckets to function
Directly public S3 buckets expose you to hotlinking, data leaks, and bypass your CDN caching
AWS charges extra fees for public S3 buckets
questions.explanation: A public S3 bucket lets anyone access your files directly — bypassing CloudFront's caching, costing you more in S3 GET requests, and exposing your data. OAC keeps S3 private while CloudFront serves it securely.

questions.question: What AWS mechanism automatically triggers the Lambda Processor when a new image is uploaded to S3?
options: A CloudWatch Events rule polling S3 every minute
An SQS queue that S3 writes to
S3 Event Notifications (s3:ObjectCreated:*)
A CloudFront trigger on the origin
questions.explanation: S3 Event Notifications fire instantly when an object is created. You configure a filter (prefix: uploads/) so only original uploads trigger the Lambda, not processed thumbnails.

questions.question: Why does the user upload images directly to S3 using a pre-signed URL instead of through the API server?
options: The API server doesn't support file uploads
It bypasses the API server to reduce latency and avoid routing large files through your compute
S3 requires direct browser connections by default
API Gateway has a 1MB payload limit
questions.explanation: Pre-signed URLs let the browser upload directly to S3, skipping your API server entirely. This avoids network bottlenecks, reduces API costs, and is faster for the user.

questions.question: What is the advantage of storing Docker images in AWS ECR over Docker Hub?
options: ECR images run faster than Docker Hub images
ECR is private, integrated with IAM, and avoids Docker Hub rate limits inside AWS
ECR supports more programming languages
Docker Hub does not support multi-stage builds
questions.explanation: ECR (Elastic Container Registry) is AWS's private Docker registry. It integrates natively with IAM for access control, eliminates Docker Hub pull rate limits (which can block CI/CD), and keeps images within the AWS network for faster pulls to EC2.

questions.question: Why is Lambda the right choice for handling Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) messages instead of the Worker?
options: Lambda is always faster than EC2 Workers
DLQ messages are rare — Lambda's pay-per-execution model avoids running a server 24/7 for rare failure events
Lambda can access DynamoDB but Workers cannot
Lambda automatically retries failed messages
questions.explanation: The DLQ only receives messages when failures occur — a rare event. Running an EC2 Worker permanently just to handle occasional DLQ messages is wasteful. Lambda runs only when triggered and you pay only for milliseconds of execution. Perfect for infrequent, event-driven tasks.

questions.question: SQS provides 'at-least-once delivery'. What must Workers implement to handle this safely?
options: Retry logic with exponential backoff
Idempotency — processing the same message twice must produce the same result
Message deduplication at the SQS level only
Circuit breakers on the API side
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery means the same message can be delivered more than once (rare, but possible). Workers must be idempotent: if a job is processed twice, the second processing should not cause duplicate side effects. This is usually handled by checking if the job is already COMPLETED in DynamoDB before processing.

questions.question: What is the SQS Visibility Timeout and why is it set to 300 seconds?
options: It deletes messages after 5 minutes
It hides a message from other Workers while one is processing it, preventing duplicate processing
It limits the message size to 300 KB
It sets the maximum retry count to 300
questions.explanation: When a Worker picks up a message, SQS makes it invisible to other Workers for the Visibility Timeout duration (5 minutes here). If the Worker finishes and deletes the message, great. If not (crash), the message reappears for retry. Set it longer than your longest expected processing time.

questions.question: What is the 'Principle of Least Privilege' in IAM?
options: Grant all permissions by default and remove as needed
Grant only the exact permissions required for a task — nothing more
Use IAM Groups instead of IAM Roles
Avoid using IAM policies for EC2 instances
questions.explanation: Least Privilege means starting with zero permissions and adding only what is strictly necessary. This limits the blast radius if credentials are compromised — an attacker can only perform actions the role explicitly allows.

questions.question: Why does the API IAM policy include 'ssm:GetParameter' for Parameter Store?
options: To store job results in SSM
To securely retrieve secrets like DB credentials and queue URLs at runtime instead of hardcoding them
SSM is required for EC2 health checks
To trigger Lambda functions via SSM
questions.explanation: Hardcoding secrets (DB passwords, queue URLs) in code is a major security risk. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store allows you to securely store secrets and fetch them at runtime. The policy grants access only to the /jobsys/* path, limiting exposure.

questions.question: Which IAM statement in the API policy ensures it can only write to the 'Jobs' table and not to other DynamoDB tables?
options: Using Effect: Deny on all other tables
Specifying the exact ARN arn:aws:dynamodb:*:*:table/Jobs in the Resource field
Adding a Condition block with TableName=Jobs
DynamoDB automatically restricts access per region
questions.explanation: By specifying the exact table ARN in the Resource field, the policy restricts the API to only that specific table. Wildcards like '*' would grant access to ALL DynamoDB tables in the account — a violation of Least Privilege.

questions.question: The API Server IAM policy includes 'sqs:SendMessage' but NOT 'sqs:DeleteMessage'. Why?
options: Deleting messages is done automatically by AWS
The API only sends messages — it never receives or deletes them (Least Privilege)
SQS does not support DeleteMessage
DeleteMessage requires a different IAM service
questions.explanation: The Principle of Least Privilege means granting only the minimum permissions needed. The API's job is to send a message to SQS — it never reads or deletes messages. Allowing DeleteMessage would be an unnecessary permission that increases risk if the role is compromised.

questions.question: Why does the Worker run as a separate process from the API Server?
options: The Worker must run on a different cloud region
Separation allows the Worker to scale independently without touching the API
AWS does not allow two containers on the same EC2 instance
The Worker needs a different operating system than the API
questions.explanation: By keeping the Worker separate, you can add more Worker instances when job volume is high without scaling the API. Each component has a single responsibility and can be deployed, scaled, and updated independently.

questions.question: What happens to an SQS message after a Worker fails to process it 3 times?
options: It is permanently deleted
It is sent back to the client
It is moved to the Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)
It is retried indefinitely
questions.explanation: The Redrive Policy sets maxReceiveCount=3. After 3 failed receive attempts, SQS automatically moves the message to the Dead Letter Queue. This prevents a 'poison-pill' message from blocking other jobs in the main queue.

questions.question: Why is DynamoDB used instead of running MySQL on an EC2 instance?
options: DynamoDB supports complex SQL JOINs
DynamoDB is fully managed — no server to patch, backup, or scale
DynamoDB is cheaper in all scenarios
DynamoDB supports stronger consistency than MySQL
questions.explanation: DynamoDB is a managed service — AWS handles replication, backups, patching, and scaling automatically. Running MySQL on EC2 would require you to manage the database server yourself, adding operational overhead.

questions.question: What is the primary role of SQS in this job processing architecture?
options: Store job results permanently
Decouple the API from the Worker so they scale independently
Provide real-time push notifications to clients
Cache API responses
questions.explanation: SQS acts as a message buffer between the API and Worker. The API drops a message and returns immediately — it doesn't wait for the job to finish. The Worker picks up messages at its own pace. This decoupling lets each component scale independently.
